basic_identification.name: School for Poetic Computation (SFPC)
basic_identification.originator: Co-founded in 2013 by Zachary Lieberman, Taeyoon Choi, Amit Pitaru, and Jen Lowe. In 2020, transitioned to collective governance by 'SFPC Stewards' after Lieberman stepped down following internal community accountability discussions around Black Lives Matter.
basic_identification.geography: New York City, with online programming. Originally held sessions in-person at various NYC venues. Post-2020, shifted to online and hybrid formats before apparent dormancy.

core_ideas.core_claim: Technology education can be poetic, critical, and community-centered rather than vocational or commercially oriented. An artist-run school can create alternative vocabulary and practice for creative technology by rejecting the optimization logic of both the tech industry and traditional academia. Code is a material for artistic and critical inquiry, not merely a professional skill.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: SFPC is specifically about the poetics of computation — treating code, electronics, hardware, and networks as artistic materials with their own aesthetics and politics. Sessions explored: code poetry, circuit bending, alternative computing histories, disability and technology, environmental sensing, and critical theory of computation. The school produced practitioners who approach digital media with a critical-poetic sensibility that differs from both commercial creative coding and academic computer science.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: Explicitly counter-attention. SFPC's pedagogy of slow learning, small cohorts, and critical reflection is antithetical to attention-economy logic. The school did not optimize for enrollment numbers, social media metrics, or career placement statistics. Sessions were intimate (typically 15-20 participants) and emphasized process over product. The school's influence spread through alumni networks and cultural osmosis rather than viral content. The very name — 'poetic computation' — signals a rejection of the instrumentalist and engagement-optimized logic of mainstream technology.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Deeply intention-native. SFPC served a declared structural need: an alternative to both MFA programs and coding bootcamps, centering artistic inquiry and critical theory alongside technical skill. The school's 2020 transition to steward governance was itself an intentional structural response to identified problems (accountability, equity, representation). Every aspect of the school's design — small cohorts, artist-run, experimental curriculum — served intentional pedagogical and political goals.

market_economics.revenue_model: Tuition-based with sliding scale and scholarships. Sessions were typically 2-10 weeks with tuition varying by program length and format. Financial aid available. Supplementary income from workshops, talks, and publications. No external institutional affiliation, endowment, or major grant funding visible. The school operated on a minimal budget with significant contributed (unpaid or under-paid) labor from founding artists and visiting faculty.
market_economics.market_position: Alternative education, not market-facing. SFPC did not sell art or operate a marketplace. Its market position was in the education space — offering an alternative to university MFA programs and commercial coding bootcamps. Alumni entered diverse careers: art practice, university teaching, tech industry creative roles, community organizing.
market_economics.price_range: Historical tuition ranged approximately from several hundred dollars (for short workshops) to several thousand dollars (for multi-week intensive sessions). Sliding scale and scholarships made participation possible for lower-income applicants. Not comparable to university tuition.
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Declining/dormant. No evidence of classes or programs offered since approximately 2022. The school appears to be on indefinite hiatus — no formal closure announcement has been found, but no new programming is visible on either website (sfpc.study or sfpc.io). The sfpc.study site still describes itself as active but shows no current offerings. GitHub repositories show minimal activity since 2021. This represents a significant decline from the school's active period (2013-2020).
market_economics.collector_demographics: Not applicable — educational institution, not a collecting platform.
market_economics.sustainability: Not sustained. The school's model — dependent on founder energy, contributed labor, small cohorts, and minimal infrastructure — proved unsustainable through the combined challenges of the 2020 accountability crisis, pandemic disruption, and the structural difficulties of artist-run organizations. The transition to collective stewardship, while principled, did not resolve the financial and organizational challenges. The apparent dormancy since 2022 suggests the model could not sustain itself without its founding energy. This is a significant finding: the most influential alternative creative-technology school of the 2010s could not sustain its operations.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: Deliberately eclectic and experimental. Sessions used: Processing, p5.js, Python, Arduino, Raspberry Pi, custom electronics, handmade circuits, found materials, poetry generators, critical theory texts, and 'anti-tools' (deliberately working with limitations and constraints). The toolchain was pedagogy-driven rather than industry-driven — tools were chosen for their ability to illuminate concepts rather than their professional utility. Some sessions explicitly rejected sophisticated tools in favor of minimal, hand-built approaches.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: Critical engagement predating the current AI moment. SFPC sessions explored machine learning, neural networks, and algorithmic systems as subjects of critical inquiry — examining bias, labor, surveillance, and power dynamics — before the ChatGPT era. The school's approach to AI would likely emphasize poetics, politics, and alternative uses rather than capability optimization. However, with no active programming since 2022, SFPC has not responded to the generative AI wave that began in late 2022.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: Performative and process-oriented. SFPC's primary 'output' was the learning experience itself — sessions, workshops, demonstrations, and student showcases. Student work ranged from interactive installations to code poetry to hardware experiments to critical essays. The emphasis on process over product means the school's aesthetic contribution is partially preserved in alumni practices and partially lost (undocumented, ephemeral learning experiences).
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Field-defining. SFPC coined or popularized: 'poetic computation,' the idea that code can be poetry and poetry can be code. The school's vocabulary bridges: critical theory (Foucault, Haraway, Hito Steyerl), creative coding practice, disability justice, environmental activism, and alternative computing histories. SFPC alumni carry this vocabulary into their subsequent work and teaching, creating a distributed influence that exceeds the school's institutional presence. The vocabulary explicitly resists instrumentalism — computation is described in terms of feeling, sensing, relating, and resisting rather than optimizing, scaling, or producing.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Maximally open (curriculum ideas freely shared, culture of openness). Maximally commons (education as commons, knowledge sharing as core value). Infrastructure over spectacle (building alternative pedagogical infrastructure, not producing spectacular outputs). Maximally collective (small cohorts, collective governance post-2020, centering BIPOC/disabled/queer makers).

infrastructure_governance.openness: High for intellectual content. Syllabi, reading lists, and session descriptions were publicly shared. The school's GitHub contained course materials. Alumni freely shared knowledge gained at SFPC. However, the actual educational experience (small-group sessions, mentorship, community) was available only to enrolled participants. The school's culture was open but its most valuable resource — the learning community — was inherently exclusive due to cohort size.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Evolved from founding-team to collective. Initially governed by the four co-founders. After the 2020 accountability crisis, transitioned to 'SFPC Stewards' — a collective governance model centering BIPOC, disabled, and queer makers. This transition was principled but appears to have been organizationally difficult — the school's reduced activity post-2020 suggests the governance transition consumed energy that previously went to programming. The collective model was explicitly a response to power concentration in the founding team.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Students owned all their creative work. The school did not operate platforms that collected or controlled student data. Course materials were shared with community consent. The school's minimal digital infrastructure meant minimal data collection.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Very low institutional interoperability. SFPC operated as a unique, self-contained educational experiment. No standardized curriculum, transferable credits, or structured relationships with other institutions. Knowledge transfer happened through people (alumni, faculty) rather than protocols or data formats.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: Minimal institutional preservation. The sfpc.io website archives past sessions, syllabi, and documentation. Some sessions produced publications or zines. The school's GitHub repositories preserve code materials. However, the most valuable aspects of SFPC (the learning community, the conversations, the process of collective inquiry) are inherently ephemeral and poorly preserved. If the school does not resume operations, much of its institutional knowledge will be preserved only in alumni memories and subsequent practices.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Community-driven consent. The 2020 transition to steward governance was fundamentally about consent — who consents to the school's direction, whose voices are centered, and how accountability operates. Within sessions, consent was managed through community agreements and facilitated discussion. No machine-readable or technically sophisticated consent architecture — consent was social and relational.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Parallel and sometimes oppositional. SFPC positioned itself against both the commercial art world and the university system. Alumni have entered the traditional art world (gallery exhibitions, museum commissions, university positions) but the school itself maintained critical distance. SFPC's pedagogy influenced university creative technology programs without becoming one itself. The school's anti-institutional stance was both a strength (radical independence) and a limitation (no institutional infrastructure for long-term sustainability).
field_position.what_it_enables: An alternative vocabulary for creative technology that centers poetics, politics, and community over optimization and production. A cohort-based learning model that creates lasting professional and personal networks among practitioners. Critical perspective on technology from within technical practice (not just theoretical critique). A pipeline of practitioners who bring critical-poetic sensibility to diverse contexts: universities, art institutions, tech companies, community organizations. Proof of concept that artist-run, alternative education models can produce significant field influence.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Institutional sustainability. Active programming (apparently dormant since 2022). Financial infrastructure. Succession planning beyond the founding team. Scale (even at peak, SFPC served hundreds of participants, not thousands). Formal documentation of its pedagogical innovations. Institutional memory that survives organizational transitions. A clear path from its educational model to participants' economic sustainability. Geographic distribution (NYC-centered).
field_position.who_is_excluded: Despite explicit commitments to equity and the post-2020 reorientation toward BIPOC/disabled/queer makers: NYC location created economic barriers (housing, travel). Cohort size limited participation to a small number per session. English-language instruction excluded non-English speakers. The school's critical-theoretical orientation assumed cultural capital and intellectual comfort with academic discourse. International participants faced visa and travel barriers. The school's apparent dormancy now excludes everyone — the model's influence persists through alumni but the educational opportunity has disappeared.
field_position.frontier_signal: Declining/dormant. Was a frontier institution from 2013-2020, defining an alternative model for creative technology education. The 2020 governance crisis and subsequent reduced activity represent a decline. The ideas and vocabulary SFPC introduced remain frontier-relevant but the institution itself is no longer active at the frontier. The question of whether SFPC can resume operations or whether its model will be carried forward by alumni and other institutions is unresolved.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Word of mouth, alumni networks, art-technology community discourse, social media (Twitter), academic citations, and coverage in art and technology press. The school's reputation spread organically through the quality of its alumni and the distinctiveness of its approach. No advertising or marketing infrastructure.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Very low. SFPC's value was in intimate, in-person educational experiences that did not depend on platform attention. The school's reputation was built through community reputation, not social media metrics. SFPC would survive (and largely did survive) the disappearance of any social media platform. However, the school used Twitter effectively to share its culture and attract applicants.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Maximally intention-native. Every aspect of SFPC served declared structural and pedagogical goals: alternative education, community building, critical inquiry, and equity. No attention-capture mechanisms. No engagement optimization. The school's anti-instrumentalist orientation was its defining characteristic.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Significant intellectual commons contribution despite limited institutional infrastructure. SFPC contributed: the vocabulary of 'poetic computation,' a model for artist-run alternative education, publicly shared syllabi and reading lists, a cohort of practitioners who carry the school's values into diverse contexts, and proof that critical-poetic approaches to technology education are viable and influential. The commons contribution is embodied in people and ideas rather than in tools, platforms, or data.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Meaning provenance through pedagogical lineage. SFPC creates provenance of ideas — participants trace their critical-poetic approach to technology back to the school. This is intellectual provenance (where did these ideas come from?) rather than ownership provenance.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Deep-historical (engaging with computing history, alternative traditions, non-Western perspectives on technology) and cyclical (session-based rhythms). The school's apparent dormancy introduces a new temporal dimension: the gap between past activity and uncertain future resumption. The school exists in a temporal limbo — neither clearly active nor clearly closed.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: SFPC was fundamentally about addressing absence — the absence of poetic, critical, and equitable approaches in technology education. The 2020 governance transition explicitly addressed the absence of BIPOC/disabled/queer voices in the school's leadership. However, the school's current dormancy creates a new absence: the loss of its active educational function. The school identified and addressed field-level absence but could not sustain the institutional structures needed to keep operating.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Coherence through shared values rather than consensus on specific positions. The school held together diverse practices (code poetry, hardware hacking, critical theory, disability justice, environmental sensing) through shared commitments to poetics, politics, and community. The 2020 governance crisis tested this coherence — the resulting transition centered specific values (BIPOC, disabled, queer leadership) that some founders may not have fully shared, creating tension between coherence and contested values.
coherence.contestability: High in principle. The 2020 governance transition was itself an act of contestation — community members contested the founding team's authority and decision-making. The transition to collective stewardship was designed to make governance more contestable. However, the school's subsequent dormancy suggests that high contestability may have contributed to organizational paralysis. The tension between contestability and operational capacity is a significant finding.
coherence.forkability: High for the model, low for the community. The SFPC model (artist-run school, poetic computation, small cohorts, critical pedagogy) can be and has been adopted by others (various creative technology workshops and programs cite SFPC as inspiration). The syllabi and reading lists are publicly available. However, the specific community of practitioners, the institutional reputation, and the network of alumni are not forkable. Several alumni have started their own educational initiatives that could be considered informal forks.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The commitment to alternative vocabulary ('poetic computation') as a way of reframing the field. The centering of equity, accessibility, and diverse voices as structural rather than supplementary concerns. The small-cohort model that creates deep relationships and shared vocabulary among practitioners. The willingness to reject instrumentalist logic even when it would make the institution more 'sustainable.' The critical engagement with technology from within technical practice. The publicly shared syllabi and pedagogical resources as commons contribution.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The unsustainable organizational model that depends on founder energy and contributed labor. The lack of financial infrastructure. The governance transition that prioritized ideological purity over organizational capacity. The geographic limitation to a single expensive city. The informal, anti-institutional ethos that prevented building the structures needed for long-term survival. The binary between radical independence and institutional sustainability — A(DAI) should seek both.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: SFPC's trajectory is a cautionary tale for A(DAI): the most influential alternative institution in the field could not sustain itself. The tension is between radical values (which SFPC embodied brilliantly) and operational sustainability (which SFPC did not achieve). A(DAI) must ask: how do we build infrastructure that carries radical values without burning out the people who hold them? SFPC's 2020 governance transition shows that addressing power and equity is essential but insufficient — it must be paired with financial sustainability and organizational resilience. The productive lesson is that A(DAI) should design for sustainability from the beginning rather than treating it as a problem to solve later.

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Minimal. As a small, informal educational organization, SFPC faced minimal regulatory burden. Not a degree-granting institution, so not subject to higher education regulation. NYC business licensing and tax requirements for any revenue. No blockchain, AI, or technology-specific regulatory exposure.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Open/informal. Course materials were generally shared freely. Students retained full IP over their work. No formal licensing framework — the culture was one of sharing rather than enclosing. Faculty contributions were not formally licensed but shared in a commons spirit.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Opt-in. Participants applied and enrolled voluntarily. The school did not collect data or include people without consent. Community agreements within sessions established norms for participation.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: Very low. SFPC operated through in-person sessions with minimal digital infrastructure. Website (basic), GitHub (course materials), Twitter (communication) — all replaceable. No dependency on any platform, blockchain, or cloud service. The school's value was in human relationships and shared physical space.
ecosystem.network_effects: Strong alumni network effects. Each cohort created a network that connected to previous cohorts, expanding the SFPC community. Alumni hired each other, collaborated, and created new educational initiatives. The school's network effects persist even in dormancy — the alumni network continues to function as a professional and creative community. SFPC functioned as a seed that produced a distributed network of practitioners.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: The crypto crash is largely irrelevant to SFPC, which was not connected to crypto markets. The more relevant trajectory is the post-2020 accountability crisis and subsequent organizational challenge. The school's decline appears driven by internal governance challenges and pandemic disruption rather than market forces. Current status: dormant with uncertain future. The ideas and community persist through alumni; the institution does not.
